ECE 6390 / Antennas and arrays

Beam to footprint

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how an angular beam becomes a ground footprint through line-of-sight geometry.

For a flat plane normal to boresight at distance r₀, a point (x, y) corresponds to u = x/√(r₀² + x² + y²) and v = y/√(r₀² + x² + y²). This maps ground coordinates into the array's angular pattern.

At small angles, footprint width is approximately range times angular width. A fixed relative angular contour therefore scales in area approximately as range squared.

An absolute coverage contour also depends on radiated power, gain normalization, receiving antenna gain, and slant-range loss. On Earth, geocentric geometry, visibility, and georeferenced cell areas replace the flat-plane approximation.

Example

A fixed 10 mrad angular width spans approximately 10 km at a distance of 1,000 km and 20 km at 2,000 km. A similarly scaled two-dimensional relative contour has four times the area.

    Practice

    1. Why does a fourfold relative-footprint area increase after doubling distance fail to establish a fourfold absolute service area?

    Track both the angular projection and received power at each ground point.

    The angular contour expands geometrically, while free-space received power falls with range squared. An absolute receiver threshold can change which parts of that expanded pattern qualify for service.
